articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a new Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This action targets individuals and entities involved in Iran's illicit activities, further restricting their access to the international financial system.

The designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing behavior in the region and its support for terrorism. Specific details of the newly designated parties and the implications of these actions were released in conjunction with the update.
This move reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to applying economic pressure on Iran to compel a change in its policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions target a network accused of providing fraudulent vessel flags and maritime certifications to Iran's shadow fleet, and a Türkiye-based company supporting sanctioned Iranian airlines.

These designations are part of Operation Economic Outcast, aiming to disrupt Iran's sanctions-evasion, aviation, and military procurement networks. The State Department also separately designated two individuals and one entity involved in efforts to procure man-portable air-defense systems for Iran.
OFAC also issued an alert regarding sanctions risks associated with falsely flagged vessels, highlighting the ongoing efforts to combat Iran's illicit shipping activities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new sanctions related to Cuba.

The Cuba-related actions include the designation of eight entities, two individuals, and the identification of five vessels as blocked property, all for supporting Cuba's oil shipping networks, state-owned entities, and military supply chains.

Additionally, OFAC published a Cuba-related determination under Executive Order 14404, authorizing sanctions against foreign persons operating in Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors, effective November 5.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal / CP24

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Updates, and Amended Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings on November 4, 2026. This action is part of the ongoing effort to counter Iran's illicit activities and its support for various malign actors.

Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert, providing guidance on potential sanctions risks. The alert aims to inform the public and financial institutions about evolving threats and compliance obligations.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, which authorizes certain transactions, financing, and other dealings involving the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA) 2020 8.5 percent bond on or after December 18, 2026. This license replaces General License 5Z and amends FAQ 595 to reflect the updated authorization.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal / Legal 500

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License for Iraq Development Bank
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026. This license authorizes the wind-down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank, and certain majority-owned entities through December 1, 2026.
Effective October 29, the amended General License FF-1 replaces and supersedes General License FF. It also includes a requirement that payments to blocked persons must be made into blocked accounts.
This amendment provides a limited period for the orderly cessation of certain activities, while ensuring continued adherence to sanctions requirements.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates North Korea IT Worker Schemes and DRC-Related Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting North Korean government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes and entities related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Specifically, OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for supporting North Korean IT worker schemes that defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the country's weapons programs. These schemes utilize fraudulent identities and deceptive tactics to secure employment.

Additionally, OFAC sanctioned the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution, for facilitating Rwanda's support for the March 23 Movement (M23) and its political wing in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. This action aims to hold Rwanda accountable under the Washington Accords and pressure it to cease support for M23.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal / Legal 500

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey.
OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. The Department of Justice also resolved a parallel investigation through a non-prosecution agreement.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Reuters / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced amendments to several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026. These updates are part of OFAC's ongoing review of published guidance to ensure information remains current.

The amended FAQs (numbers 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) cover topics related to blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC. This includes clarifications on when to block an account or transfer, interest requirements on blocked funds, and when to reject a transaction instead of blocking it.

The revisions also provide clearer explanations of reporting mechanics, including that both blocked-property reports and rejected-transaction reports must be filed through the OFAC Reporting System (ORS) within ten business days of the relevant blocking or rejection.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center / Compliance Cohort

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related, Russia-Related General Licenses; Removes Belarus, North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

In addition to these actions, OFAC announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. This indicates a dynamic approach to sanctions, with adjustments made based on evolving geopolitical circumstances and compliance considerations.
The issuance of new General Licenses aims to provide clarity and authorization for specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions regimes.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA)
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

The PAIPA aims to combat the theft of American intellectual property and impose sanctions on those involved in such illicit activities. The new designations target individuals and entities found to be undermining U.S. intellectual property rights.

The accompanying General Licenses provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that might otherwise be prohibited, ensuring that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted by the new designations.

articles.headline: EU Strengthens Sanctions Against Russia and Belarus with 21st Package
body: The European Union has adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia and Belarus, with measures coming into effect on November 5, 2026. This package includes new sanctions and sector-specific measures targeting the Russian energy and financial sectors, as well as measures to strengthen legal protection for European individuals and companies.

The new measures target 33 Russian banks, one bank from a third country, 17 financial institutions and crypto service providers, five companies from third countries, four Russian airports, and two Russian ports. Additionally, 41 vessels linked to the Russian shadow fleet are now subject to comprehensive bans on purchases, sales, and the provision of services.

The EU's Sanctions Envoy, David O'Sullivan, convened the eighth Sanctions Coordinators Forum to discuss common efforts to further constrain Russia's financing via payment networks in third countries, analyze circumvention trends, and examine Russia's energy exports and the operations of the shadow fleet.

articles.headline: UK Sanctions List Updated with Correction for Zenith Global Corporation Limited
body: On November 3, 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List on GOV.UK with a correction related to Zenith Global Corporation Limited.

The correction is an administrative amendment, clarifying details for the entity which remains subject to asset freeze, trust services sanctions, director disqualification sanction, and transport sanctions under The Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019.

The transport sanctions prohibit ships and aircraft owned, controlled, chartered, or operated by a designated person from entering or overflying the UK, and also include a prohibition on technical assistance related to such aircraft and ships.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of OFAC sanctions. The violations involved exporting networking equipment and related services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer between September 2018 and March 2022.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. The settlement amount reflects OFAC's consideration of aggravating factors, including reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and actual knowledge of transactions with the sanctioned party.

This action emphasizes the importance of sanctions-related diligence before acquiring a company or its assets, remaining vigilant regarding sanctions risks thereafter, and ensuring adequate oversight of foreign activities and operations.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to an $11,662,930 settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for 475 apparent sanctions violations. These violations occurred between September 2021 and April 2025 and involved transactions totaling approximately $14.8 million across various sanctions programs, including those related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The OFAC settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which imposed over $1.21 billion in combined penalties for anti-money laundering and sanctions failures.

OFAC classified the violations as non-egregious and mostly not voluntarily disclosed. The failures included issues with vendor data, delayed updates to screening filters, analyst errors, and alert suppression rules, particularly concerning transactions routed through blocked banks.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 OFAC Civil Penalty for Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The settlement resolves four apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Regulations and six apparent violations of the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus dealt in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which had been sanctioned for selling pill presses to counterfeit-pill makers. Pegasus also failed to respond fully to an OFAC subpoena for six months.

OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed. The case highlights the importance of thorough screening beyond just names, especially for freight forwarders and customs brokers.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: An individual has agreed to pay a civil monetary penalty of $1,427,230 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The details of the individual's identity and the specific sanctions program violated were not immediately disclosed in the public summary, but such penalties underscore OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions across all sectors and against individuals.
This enforcement action serves as a reminder that individuals, as well as corporations, are subject to OFAC's regulations and can face significant penalties for non-compliance.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764 Over Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer of weighing equipment, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its and its Italian subsidiary's potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

The apparent violations occurred between July 2019 and November 2021, when Rice Lake's Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with the knowledge that these goods were ultimately destined for an end-user in Iran.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and non-egregious. The case highlights the importance of ensuring that foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions, even when dealing with third-country distributors.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has agreed to pay a civil monetary penalty of $1,050,000 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The specific details of the violations leading to this penalty were not immediately available in the public summary. However, the substantial amount indicates serious compliance deficiencies that resulted in prohibited transactions.

This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued focus on ensuring that U.S. companies, including consulting firms, maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent engagement in illicit activities.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Faces $275,000,000 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Adani Enterprises Limited has been assessed a significant civil monetary penalty of $275,000,000 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This substantial penalty addresses apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The specific nature of the violations leading to this large penalty was not detailed in the public summary. However, a penalty of this magnitude typically indicates a pattern of serious and egregious conduct, or transactions involving significant value with sanctioned parties.

This enforcement action highlights OFAC's readiness to impose severe penalties on major international entities that fail to adhere to U.S. sanctions laws, emphasizing the critical need for comprehensive compliance frameworks.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has agreed to pay a civil monetary penalty of $1,110,661 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The specific details of the violations were not immediately available in the public summary. However, the penalty indicates that the financial services firm engaged in transactions that were prohibited under OFAC's various sanctions programs.

This action underscores the importance for financial institutions to implement robust sanctions screening and compliance programs to prevent facilitating transactions with sanctioned individuals or entities.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 Over Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations. These violations occurred between 2018 and 2021.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination regarding the nature and extent of the individual's involvement in prohibited transactions related to Syria.
This case highlights OFAC's enforcement reach against individuals, emphasizing that U.S. sanctions laws apply to U.S. persons regardless of their location.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 OFAC Civil Penalty for Kingpin Act Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements with two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act and processed 89 related financial transactions for the benefit of the designees' children.

OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List. Aggravating factors included reckless disregard for sanctions requirements and actual knowledge of transactional activity with the sanctioned parties.

Mitigating considerations included IMG Academy's lack of prior violations, prompt and substantial cooperation, and the implementation of a formal sanctions compliance program following an ownership change. This case serves as a warning to academic institutions with international student bodies and foreign payors.

Maintaining sanctions remains critical to limiting windfall revenues for Russia, especially given the current energy market dynamics.
The growth in the Russian economy has already slowed significantly, from 4.9% in 2024 to 1% in 2025, and is expected to remain subdued in 2026 and 2027, at near-stagnation levels.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in northern Spain
body: Officers attended the scene in connection with a separate incident at a residential building in the Spanish city.

articles.headline: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
body: The Israeli military says its soldiers opened fire at individuals “who intended to hurl stones” at a road used by Israelis.

articles.headline: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
body: With 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and joined the fight against the occupying German forces.

articles.headline: Oxford museum returns ancestral Naga skulls to India
body: The remains will be taken to Nagaland, where tribal leaders plan a joint memorial and burial.

articles.headline: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
body: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.

articles.headline: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
body: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.

articles.headline: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
body: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.

articles.headline: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
body: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.

articles.headline: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
body: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.

articles.headline: Watch: Man smashes Chinese government building with excavator
body: Police say they have detained a 47-year-old suspect and no one was injured in the incident.

articles.headline: Dana White declines Trump’s offer to be White House press secretary
body: In a social media post over the weekend, the president asked the UFC boss to take over the role, but later said he was "having a little fun".

articles.headline: Millions fill Buenos Aires streets to welcome Pope Leo XIV
body: The Pope celebrated an outdoor Mass in Argentina's capital, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, just three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
